title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Issuing the Tenth Batch of Guiding Cases
ruling_gist_en: An operator of internet services, by forcibly popping up advertisements on the search result pages of other operators' websites, violates the principle of good faith and generally recognized business ethics, hinders the legitimate operation of other operators, and damages their lawful rights and interests. Such act may be deemed as unfair competition in accordance with the principle provision of Article 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China.
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Notice on Publishing the Tenth Batch of Guiding Cases

Fa [2015] No. 85

High People's Courts of all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government; the Military Court of the People's Liberation Army; and the Production and Construction Corps Branch of the High People's Court of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region:

In accordance with Article 9 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Case Guidance Work, the Supreme People's Court has sorted and compiled cases published in the Supreme People's Court Gazette that have guiding significance for the trial and enforcement work of courts nationwide. Upon discussion and decision by the Adjudication Committee of the Supreme People's Court, the following eight cases (Guiding Cases No. 45-52), including the dispute over unfair competition between Beijing Baidu Netcom Science Technology Co., Ltd. v. Qingdao Aoshang Network Technology Co., Ltd. et al., which have been sorted and compiled, are hereby published as the tenth batch of guiding cases for reference when trying similar cases.

April 15, 2015

Guiding Case No. 45: Beijing Baidu Netcom Science Technology Co., Ltd. v. Qingdao Aoshang Network Technology Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over unfair competition

(Approved by the Adjudication Committee of the Supreme People's Court and published on April 15, 2015)

Keywords: Civil; unfair competition; network services; principle of good faith

Ruling Gist

An operator engaged in internet services that forcibly displays advertisements on the search result pages of another operator's website, thereby violating the principle of good faith and generally accepted commercial ethics, obstructing the legitimate business of other operators, and harming their lawful rights and interests, may be deemed to constitute unfair competition in accordance with the principle provisions of Article 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China.

Relevant Legal Provision

Article 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

The plaintiff, Beijing Baidu Netcom Science Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Baidu Company), alleged that its website www.baidu.com (hereinafter referred to as the Baidu website) is a Chinese-language search engine website. The three defendants, Qingdao Aoshang Network Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Aoshang Network Company), China United Network Communications Co., Ltd., Qingdao Branch (hereinafter referred to as Unicom Qingdao Company), and China United Network Communications Co., Ltd., Shandong Branch (hereinafter referred to as Unicom Shandong Company), utilizing the internet access network services of China Netcom in the Qingdao area of Shandong Province, forcibly added advertisements on the search result pages of Baidu Company's website. This conduct damaged Baidu Company's goodwill and economic benefits, violated the principle of good faith, and constituted unfair competition. Baidu Company requested the court to: 1. declare that the conduct of Aoshang Network Company and Unicom Qingdao Company constituted unfair competition against the plaintiff, order them to cease such unfair competition, and hold the third party jointly and severally liable; 2. order the three defendants to publish statements in newspapers to eliminate the adverse effects; 3. order the three defendants to jointly compensate the plaintiff for economic losses of RMB 4.8 million and reasonable expenses of RMB 100,000 incurred in this case.

The defendant, Aoshang Network Company, argued that it did not engage in unfair competition and should not be required to apologize or pay RMB 4.8 million in compensation.

The defendant, Unicom Qingdao Company, argued that the plaintiff had no evidence to prove that it had committed the alleged conduct, had not submitted evidence to prove actual losses suffered, and that there was no competitive relationship between the plaintiff and itself. It requested that all of the plaintiff's claims be dismissed.

The defendant, Unicom Shandong Company, argued that the plaintiff had no evidence to prove that it had committed the alleged unfair competition or infringement, and that there was no legal basis for holding it jointly and severally liable.

The third party, Qingdao Pengfei International Air Travel Service Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Pengfei Airlines), stated that this case was unrelated to the third party.

The court found through trial that: Baidu Company's business scope includes internet information services, and it operates the Baidu website at the approved domain name www.baidu.com, primarily providing internet information search services to network users. Aoshang Network Company's business scope includes network engineering construction, network technology application services, computer software design and development, etc., and its website is www.og.com.cn. On the "Company Overview" page of the said website, it stated that it owned four websites: China Aoshang Net (www.og.com.cn), Ode Network Marketing Partner (www.og.net.cn), Qingdao Telephone Real Name Net (www.0532114.org), and Peninsula Talent Net (www.job17.com). On its website, when introducing its "Network Direct Access" service, it stated: no plug-in installation required, advertising pages appear forcibly. When introducing the product form of "Search Pass," it listed the following steps in text and images: Step 1: enter keywords in the search engine dialog box; Step 2: priority display of Network Direct Access advertising slot (5-second display); Step 3: simultaneously click on the above advertising slot to directly enter a new window of the promotional website; Step 4: after 5 seconds, the original window automatically displays the search results from the first step. The website also introduced the above services in other forms. Unicom Qingdao Company's business scope includes internet access services and information services, and Qingdao Information Port (domain name qd.sd.cn) is its owned website. "Telephone Real Name" is a voice search service jointly operated by Unicom Qingdao Company and Aoshang Network Company, and the website at www.0532114.org, "114 Telephone Real Name Voice Search," indicates that the copyright owner of the website is Unicom Qingdao Company, and the exclusive registration center is Aoshang Network Company. Unicom Shandong Company's business scope includes internet access services and information services. Its website (www.sdcnc.cn) shows that Unicom Qingdao Company is its subordinate branch. Pengfei Airlines' business scope includes airline ticket sales agency services, etc.

On April 14, 2009, Baidu Company discovered that when accessing the internet through the Qingdao City, Shandong Province China Netcom connection and logging into the Baidu website (www.baidu.com), after entering "Pengfei Airlines" in the search dialog box and clicking "Baidu It," a page displaying "Discounted tickets grab first, just dial 114" popped up. Upon quickly clicking this page, a page with the address http://air.qd.sd.cn/ was opened. After entering "Qingdao Talent Network" and clicking "Baidu It," a page displaying "Find good jobs at Peninsula Talent Network www.job17.com" popped up. Upon quickly clicking "Click Now" displayed on that page, a page with the address http://www.job17.com/ was opened. After entering "Telephone Real Name" and clicking "Baidu It," a page displaying "Check information dial 114, voice search is easier to use" popped up, and then that page redirected to the corresponding "Telephone Real Name" search result page. The agent ad litem of Baidu Company used a notary public's computer to notarize the process of logging into Baidu search and other websites, and the notarial deed recorded the foregoing content. Expert opinion indicated that the linked website (http://air.qd.sd.cn/) shared the same domain (qd.sd.cn) with Unicom Shandong Company's subordinate website Qingdao Information Port (www.qd.sd.cn), and the website air.qd.sd.cn belonged to the Qingdao site under Unicom Shandong Company's subordinate website.

Judgment

The Qingdao Intermediate People's Court of Shandong Province rendered civil judgment (2009) Qing Min San Chu Zi No. 110 on September 2, 2009: 1. Aoshang Network Company and Unicom Qingdao Company shall immediately cease the unfair competition conduct against Baidu Company upon the effective date of this judgment, i.e., they shall not use technical means to cause advertisement pages of Aoshang Network Company and Unicom Qingdao Company to pop up when network users who access the internet through Unicom Qingdao Company's internet access services log into the Baidu website for keyword searches; 2. Aoshang Network Company and Unicom Qingdao Company shall, within ten days of the effective date of this judgment, compensate Baidu Company for economic losses of RMB 200,000; 3. Aoshang Network Company and Unicom Qingdao Company shall, within ten days of the effective date of this judgment, publish statements on the homepage of their respective websites to eliminate the adverse effects, with the statements to be displayed for fifteen consecutive days; 4. Baidu Company's other claims are dismissed. After the judgment was pronounced, Unicom Qingdao Company and Aoshang Network Company appealed. The Shandong High People's Court rendered civil judgment (2010) Lu Min San Zhong Zi No. 5-2 on March 20, 2010, dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that: In this case, Baidu Company sued Aoshang Network Company, Unicom Qingdao Company, and Unicom Shandong Company, requesting that they cease the unfair competition conduct and bear corresponding civil liability. Accordingly, whether the plaintiff's claims could be established should be determined by the following steps: 1. whether the defendants committed the alleged conduct; 2. if the alleged conduct was committed, whether it constituted unfair competition; 3. if it constituted unfair competition, how to bear civil liability.

I. Whether the defendants committed the alleged conduct

Domain names are hierarchical character identifiers used to identify and locate computers on the internet. Based on the facts found, www.job17.com is the Peninsula Talent website owned by Aoshang Network Company, and "Telephone Real Name Voice Search" is a service jointly operated by Unicom Qingdao Company and Aoshang Network Company. The domain name qd.sd.cn is owned by Unicom Qingdao Company and is actually used as the domain name for "Qingdao Information Port." air.qd.sd.cn, as a subdomain of qd.sd.cn, is allocated and managed by its parent domain qd.sd.cn. Unicom Qingdao Company, as the holder of the domain name qd.sd.cn, denied ownership of the domain name air.qd.sd.cn but did not provide evidence to prove it. Therefore, it should be determined that at the time of notarization preservation, the user of this subdomain was Unicom Qingdao Company.

When logging into a search engine website for keyword searches on the internet, the normal result should be the search result page of the search engine website, and no other pages unrelated to the search engine website should pop up. However, within the network access service area provided by Unicom Qingdao Company, the phenomenon of forcibly popping up advertising pages unrelated to the search results occurred. The popping up of such advertising pages was not caused by the programs installed on the notary public's computer that accessed the internet. Unicom Qingdao Company neither provided evidence to prove that the same situation would occur in other network access service providers' areas nor gave a reasonable explanation for the above situation occurring within its network access service area. Therefore, it could be determined that within the area where Unicom Qingdao Company provides internet access services, human intervention was made to the search requests sent by network service users to the Baidu website, causing the advertising pages that the intervener intended to publish to forcibly appear before the normal search result pages.

Regarding the issue of the entity that implemented the above intervention, based on the facts found, Aoshang Network Company's introduction of its "Network Direct Access" service on its homepage showed that the description of the forcible pop-up of advertisements was entirely consistent with the form notarized and preserved, and the pop-up advertising pages "Peninsula Talent Network" and "114 Telephone Voice Search" that appeared during the notarization preservation were all websites or services it was operating. Therefore, Aoshang Network Company was the beneficiary of the intervention. In the absence of evidence provided by Aoshang Network Company showing that there were other entities implementing the above advertising conduct for it, it could be determined that Aoshang Network Company was the entity that implemented the above intervention.

Regarding the issue of whether Unicom Qingdao Company was the entity that committed the alleged infringing conduct, the intervention by Aoshang Network Company was not achieved by installing plug-ins, programs, or the like on client computers, but could be achieved within a specific network access service area. Therefore, such conduct could not be realized without the cooperation of the network access service provider. Unicom Qingdao Company did not provide evidence to prove that Aoshang Network Company had implemented the above conduct through illegal means of interfering with its internet access services. Furthermore, Unicom Qingdao Company was the owner of the domain name air.qd.sd.cn, and the liability for infringing upon others' lawful rights and interests due to holding or using a domain name is borne by the domain name holder. Unicom Qingdao Company and Aoshang Network Company jointly operated the telephone real name business, meaning that Unicom Qingdao Company was also a beneficiary of the above conduct. Therefore, it could be determined that Unicom Qingdao Company was also an entity that implemented the above intervention.

Regarding whether Unicom Shandong Company implemented the intervention, since Unicom Shandong Company and Unicom Qingdao Company are both branches of China United Network Communications Co., Ltd., there was no evidence to prove that they had a relationship of one establishing the other, nor was there evidence to prove that Unicom Shandong Company participated in implementing the intervention. Unicom Qingdao Company, as a civil entity, has the qualification to bear civil liability. Therefore, the claims against Unicom Shandong Company were not supported. Baidu Company named Pengfei Airlines as a third party in this case, but in the complaint and during the trial, it did not allege that the third party had engaged in unfair competition, nor did it request the third party to bear civil liability. Therefore, naming Pengfei Airlines as a third party was an improper designation of parties, and it was not supported.

II. Whether the alleged infringing conduct constituted unfair competition

Articles 5 to 15 of Chapter II of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Anti-Unfair Competition Law) list types of unfair competition conduct. For conduct not listed in specific provisions, it can only be deemed unfair competition if it can be determined to violate the principle provisions of Article 2 of the same law in accordance with generally accepted commercial ethics and common understanding. To determine whether an operator's conduct constitutes unfair competition, the following aspects should be considered: first, the actor is an operator within the meaning of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law; second, when engaging in commercial activities, the operator fails to follow the principles of voluntariness, equality, fairness, and good faith, violating the provisions of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law and generally accepted commercial ethics; third, the operator's unfair competition conduct harms the lawful rights and interests of legitimate operators.

First, according to the definition of operators in Article 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, the determination of an operator does not require that the plaintiff and defendant belong to the same industry or service category. Any market entity engaged in the sale of goods or profit-making services may be considered an operator. Unicom Qingdao Company, Aoshang Network Company, and Baidu Company are all market entities engaged in internet business and are operators within the meaning of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law. Although Unicom Qingdao Company is an internet access service operator and Baidu Company is a search service operator, and their service categories are not entirely identical, the commercial conduct of Unicom Qingdao Company in popping up advertisements before the appearance of Baidu search results constitutes a competitive relationship with Baidu Company's paid search model.

Second, operators who have commercial connections in market competition and, in violation of the principle of good faith and generally accepted commercial ethics, improperly obstruct the legitimate business of other operators and harm the lawful rights and interests of other operators, may be deemed to constitute unfair competition in accordance with the principle provisions of Article 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law. Although publishing advertisements and conducting commercial activities on the internet differ significantly from traditional business models, operators engaged in internet business should still gain competitive advantages through honest management and fair competition. They cannot use the service conduct or market share of others to operate and profit without permission. The conduct of Unicom Qingdao Company and Aoshang Network Company exploited the advantage of the Baidu website's search engine being widely used by internet users in China. They used technical means to cause, when network users accessing the internet through Unicom Qingdao Company's internet access services logged into the Baidu website for keyword searches, advertising pages closely related to the searched keywords and content to forcibly appear before normal search results. This conduct induced network users who might have been expected to search for relevant information through Baidu Company's search results to click on the advertising pages, affecting Baidu Company's provision of paid search services and promotional services to network users. It constituted using the search services provided by Baidu Company to profit for itself. This conduct neither obtained Baidu Company's consent nor complied with the will of users using its internet access services. It could easily lead internet users to mistakenly believe that the pop-up advertising pages were made by Baidu Company, which could lower internet users' evaluation of the services provided by Baidu Company and adversely affect Baidu Company's commercial reputation, harming Baidu Company's lawful rights and interests. At the same time, it also violated the principle of good faith and generally accepted commercial ethics, thus constituting unfair competition.

III. Regarding the bearing of civil liability

Since Unicom Qingdao Company and Aoshang Network Company jointly committed the unfair competition conduct, they shall bear joint and several liability in accordance with Article 130 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China. In accordance with Article 134 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 20 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, they shall bear civil liability for ceasing the infringement, compensating for losses, and eliminating adverse effects. First, Aoshang Network Company and Unicom Qingdao Company shall immediately cease the unfair competition conduct, i.e., they shall not use technical means to cause advertising pages of the two defendants to pop up when network users accessing the internet through Unicom Qingdao Company's internet access services log into the Baidu website for keyword searches. Second, taking into account the reasonable expenses incurred by the plaintiff in this case, the circumstances of the defendants' unfair competition conduct, and the duration of such conduct, the court discretionally orders the two defendants to jointly compensate for economic losses of RMB 200,000. Finally, when internet users log into Baidu for searches and encounter pop-up advertising pages, they will typically believe that such conduct is by Baidu Company. Therefore, the conduct of the two defendants caused certain negative impacts on Baidu Company, and they shall bear civil liability for eliminating adverse effects. Since the conduct occurred on the internet and within the area where Unicom Qingdao Company provides internet access services, it is determined that the two defendants shall publish an announcement on the homepage of their respective websites to eliminate the adverse effects.

Guiding Case No. 46: Shandong Lujin Industrial Co., Ltd. v. Juancheng County Lujin Arts & Crafts Co., Ltd. and Jining Lizhibang Home Textile Co., Ltd. — dispute over trademark infringement and unfair competition

(Approved by the Adjudication Committee of the Supreme People's Court and published on April 15, 2015)

Keywords: Civil; trademark infringement; unfair competition; generic name of goods

Ruling Gist

When determining whether a name with regional characteristics constitutes a generic name for goods, comprehensive analysis should be conducted with attention to the following aspects: (1) the name is established by convention in a certain region or field, has been commonly used for a long time, and is recognized by relevant public; (2) the production process of the goods referred to by the name has been formed through the long-term collective labor practice of the people in a certain region or field; (3) the raw materials for the production of the goods referred to by the name are commonly produced in a certain region or field.

Relevant Legal Provision

Article 59 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

Plaintiff Shandong Lujin Industrial Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Lujin Company) alleged that the defendants, Juancheng County Lujin Arts and Crafts Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Juancheng Lujin Company) and Jining Lizhibang Home Textiles Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Lizhibang Company), had produced and sold in large quantities Lujin products bearing the characters "Lujin", thereby infringing its exclusive right to use the registered trademark "Lujin". The enterprise name of Juancheng Lujin Company contained the plaintiff's registered trademark "Lujin", misleading consumers and constituting unfair competition. "Lujin" was not a generic name. The plaintiff requested that the court order the two defendants to bear legal liability for infringing the exclusive right to use a registered trademark and for unfair competition.

Defendant Juancheng Lujin Company argued that before the plaintiff Lujin Company was established and before the registration of the Lujin trademark was completed, "Lujin" had already become a generic name. In accordance with relevant regulations, its use constituted "fair use" and did not constitute trademark infringement or unfair competition.

Defendant Lizhibang Company did not answer at first instance, but appealed at second instance, arguing that "Lujin" was a generic name for folk handwoven cotton textiles in the southwestern Shandong area, and that it was not aware that "Lujin" was a registered trademark of Lujin Company. After receiving the complaint, it had ceased the relevant use, and therefore should not bear liability for damages.

The court found the following facts upon trial: The predecessor of Lujin Company, Jiaxiang County Ruijin Folk Arts and Crafts Factory, obtained the word trademark "Lujin" under Registration No. 1345914 on December 21, 1999, with a validity period from December 21, 1999 to December 20, 2009, approved for use on goods in Class 25, including clothing, shoes, and hats. Lujin Company also obtained a combined trademark "Lj+LUJIN" under Registration No. 1665032 on November 14, 2001, with a validity period from November 14, 2001 to November 13, 2011, approved for use on goods in Class 24, including "textile fabrics, cotton fabrics, fabrics for underwear, gauze, textiles, terry cloth, non-woven fabrics, bath towels, bed sheets, textile furniture covers, etc." Jiaxiang County Ruijin Folk Arts and Crafts Factory changed its name to Jiaxiang County Lujin Industrial Co., Ltd. on February 9, 2001, and later to Shandong Lujin Industrial Co., Ltd. on June 11, 2007.

After obtaining the exclusive right to use the registered trademark "Lujin", Lujin Company repeatedly advertised its products and registered trademark in various media, and was admitted as a member unit of the "China Time-honored Brand" Working Committee in March 2006. Through years of effort and extensive advertising and market promotion, its "Lujin" brand series of products, especially "Lujin" brand clothing, enjoyed a certain reputation in China. On November 16, 2006, the "Lujin" registered trademark was certified as a well-known trademark of Shandong Province.

In March 2007, Lujin Company purchased from Lizhibang Lujin Specialty Store products identical or similar to the goods approved for use with the Lujin registered trademark, produced by Juancheng Lujin Company. The labels (hang tags), packaging boxes, packaging bags, and the storefront of the products all bore the characters "Lujin". On the storefront, "Lujin" was prominently enlarged, and the invoice issued bore the official seal of Lizhibang Company.

Juancheng Lujin Company was established on March 3, 2003, and the trademark used on its products was a combined trademark of "Jingyifang characters + graphic", which had been applied for registration but not yet approved. In September 2007, Juancheng Lujin Company applied for cancellation of Lujin Company's registered trademark No. 1345914 "Lujin", which was accepted by the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board under the State Administration for Industry and Commerce, but no ruling had been made.

At the request of Lujin Company, the court of first instance lawfully preserved evidence against Juancheng Lujin Company and Lizhibang Company, discovering that both defendants had in stock large quantities of goods of the same or similar type as those approved for use with the "Lujin" registered trademark. The labels (hang tags), packaging boxes, packaging bags, price tags, and the storefronts of the defendants all bore the plaintiff's registered trademark "Lujin". On the labels (hang tags), packaging boxes, and packaging bags of the allegedly infringing goods, the characters "Lujin" were enlarged and prominently used as the name or decoration of the goods, and the packaging bags did not indicate the manufacturer or its address.

It was further ascertained that folk brocade in southwestern Shandong is a type of folk handwoven cotton textile from Shandong, named for its colorful and splendid patterns resembling brocade. It has a history of over a thousand years in the southwestern Shandong area and is part of the long-standing Qilu culture. Beginning in the mid-1980s, the development and utilization of southwestern Shandong brocade began. On January 8, 1986, an "Exhibition and Report Meeting on Southwestern Shandong Brocade and Modern Life" was held in Jinan. On August 20, 1986, an "Exhibition of Lujin and Modern Life" was held at the Cultural Palace of Nationalities in Beijing. Around 1986, newspapers such as People's Daily, Economic Reference, and Farmers' Daily published special reports on "Lujin", and China Central Television and Shandong Television also produced several special programs on "Lujin". Since then, "Lujin" has been widely used as a general term for Shandong folk handwoven cotton textiles. Subsequently, research, development, and production of Lujin gradually spread and continued to grow. On November 15, 1987, to promote the further integration of Lujin culture with modern life, the Canadian International Development Agency (CIDA) and the All-China Women's Federation jointly held a bilateral cooperation project—the Juancheng Yangtun Women's Lujin Textile Cooperative Training Class in Yangtun Village, Juancheng County.

Local chronicles and historical records from Shandong Province, Jinan, Heze, and other areas, when discussing history, local specialties, or traditional crafts, frequently mention "Lujin", consistently regarding it as a traditional textile product primarily made of cotton yarn, popular in the vast rural areas of southwestern Shandong, and one of the main folk art forms of Shandong. Relevant reference books and publications also introduce "Lujin", all describing it as Shandong folk handwoven patterned cotton cloth, with cotton as the main raw material, hand-spun, dyed, and woven, commonly known as "coarse cloth" or "handwoven cloth", and because of its colorful and brocade-like patterns, it is called "Lujin".

On December 25, 1995, the Shandong Provincial Cultural Relics Bureau issued an "Official Reply on the Construction of the 'China Lujin Museum'", approving the establishment of the "China Lujin Museum" in Juancheng County by the Heze Regional Cultural Bureau. On December 23, 2006, the Shandong Provincial People's Government announced the first batch of provincial-level intangible cultural heritage, among which the "Lujin Folk Handicraft Technique" submitted by the Shandong Provincial Department of Culture, Juancheng County, and Jiaxiang County was designated as intangible cultural heritage. On June 7, 2008, the State Council, in Document Guo Fa [2008] No. 19, determined that the "Lujin Weaving Technique" submitted by Juancheng County and Jiaxiang County of Shandong Province was included in the second batch of the national intangible cultural heritage list.

Judgment

The Intermediate People's Court of Jining City, Shandong Province, on August 25, 2008, rendered a civil judgment (2007) Ji Min Wu Chu Zi No. 6: 1. Juancheng Lujin Company shall immediately cease using "Lujin" as a product name or product decoration on its produced and sold clothing products in Class 25 from the date the judgment took effect, and shall eliminate the "Lujin" characters from its existing allegedly infringing products within 30 days from the date the judgment took effect; Lizhibang Company shall immediately cease selling the allegedly infringing products produced by Juancheng Lujin Company. 2. Juancheng Lujin Company shall compensate Lujin Company for economic losses of 250,000 yuan within 15 days from the date the judgment took effect; Lizhibang Company shall compensate Lujin Company for economic losses of 10,000 yuan. 3. Juancheng Lujin Company shall change its enterprise name within 30 days from the date the judgment took effect, and the changed enterprise name shall not include the characters "Lujin"; Lizhibang Company shall immediately eliminate the "Lujin" characters from its storefront from the date the judgment took effect. After the judgment was pronounced, Juancheng Lujin Company and Lizhibang Company appealed. The High People's Court of Shandong Province, on August 5, 2009, rendered a civil judgment (2009) Lu Min San Zhong Zi No. 34: reversing the civil judgment (2007) Ji Min Wu Chu Zi No. 6 of the Intermediate People's Court of Jining City, Shandong Province; and dismissing the claims of Lujin Company.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that, based on the facts of this case, it could be determined that before Lujin Company registered "Lujin" as a trademark in 1999, it had already become a generic name for Shandong folk handwoven cotton textiles, and the "Lujin" weaving technique was an intangible cultural heritage. The conduct of Juancheng Lujin Company and Jining Lizhibang Company did not constitute trademark infringement or unfair competition.

First, "Lujin" had become a generic name for cotton textiles with regional characteristics. A generic name for goods refers to the common designation of a certain product as established by industry standards or social conventions. This generic name can be a designation prescribed by industry standards or an abbreviation established by public convention. Lujin refers to folk handwoven brocade made of pure cotton from southwestern Shandong, with colorful and splendid patterns resembling brocade, and has a history of over a thousand years in the southwestern Shandong area. "Lujin", as a generic name for handwoven textiles with Shandong characteristics, was recognized by major national media, various professional newspapers, and Shandong news media. The provincial, municipal, and county chronicles of Shandong, Jining, Heze, Jiaxiang, and Juancheng all record "Lujin" as a "new name" for traditional southwestern Shandong folk brocade. Reference books on arts and crafts also confirm that "Lujin" is a folk handwoven cotton textile produced in Shandong. The weaving technique of "Lujin" has a long history; when "Lujin" is mentioned, people think of the traditional and time-honored Shandong folk handwoven cotton textiles and their weaving technique. The "Lujin weaving technique" was designated as a national intangible cultural heritage. The production process of pure cotton handwoven textiles represented by "Lujin" was not invented by any individual or legal entity but was formed through long-term labor practice by the people of the Shandong region, especially the southwestern Shandong area. The raw materials for the pure cotton handwoven textiles represented by "Lujin" are not specifically cultivated by any individual or legal entity but are cotton widely planted in various regions of Shandong. Since the mid-1980s, through extensive media promotion, "Lujin" had become a general term for folk handwoven textiles in the Shandong region, mainly using cotton as raw material, hand-spun, dyed, and woven, and was commonly used within the textile industry in Shandong and accepted by the relevant public. In summary, it could be determined that "Lujin" was a generic name for folk pure cotton handwoven textiles in the Shandong region, especially southwestern Shandong.

Regarding Lujin Company's claim that the name "Lujin" was not widespread, and that although coarse cloth is produced in other parts of China, it is not called "Lujin", the court held that for generic names of goods with regional characteristics, the determination of their widespread nature should be based on the specific production area and the relevant public, rather than nationwide. The fact that handwoven cotton textiles in other provinces of China are not called "Lujin" does not affect the fact that "Lujin" specifically refers to the unique folk handwoven cotton textile of the Shandong region. Regarding Lujin Company's claim that "Lujin" was not scientific, as cotton textiles should be called "cotton" rather than "brocade", the court held that there is no necessary relationship between the determination of a name and its scientific nature. For a name that has been accepted by the relevant public, refers to a clear concept, and is established by convention, even if it lacks scientific precision, it does not prevent it from being a generic name. Regarding Lujin Company's further claim that "Lujin" was not universal, as some operators and consumers in Shandong Province refer to such folk handwoven cotton textiles as "coarse cloth" or "old native cloth", the court held that the appellation "Lujin" is a new name established in the mid-1980s, and after years of promotion and use, it had become known and accepted by the relevant public. The existence of older names such as "coarse cloth" and "old native cloth" does not affect the determination of "Lujin" as a generic name.

Second, where a registered trademark contains a generic name for the goods, the holder of the exclusive right to use the registered trademark has no right to prohibit others from fair use. Article 49 of the Regulations on the Implementation of the Trademark Law of the PRC provides: "Where a registered trademark contains a generic name, figure, or model of the goods, or directly indicates the quality, main raw materials, function, purpose, weight, quantity, or other characteristics of the goods, or contains a place name, the holder of the exclusive right to use the registered trademark has no right to prohibit others from fair use." The main function of a trademark is to distinguish, i.e., to enable consumers to distinguish the providers of different goods or services based on different trademarks. The purpose of protecting trademark rights is to prevent confusion as to the source of goods or services. Since the "Lujin" word trademark and the "Lj+LUJIN" combined trademark of Lujin Company were identical to the generic name "Lujin" for Shandong folk handwoven cotton textiles, their inherent distinctiveness was thereby weakened. Although "Lujin" was not a generic name for Lujin clothing, it was a generic name for Shandong folk handwoven cotton textiles. The trademark registrant does not enjoy exclusive rights to the generic part of a trademark, and does not affect others' fair use of "Lujin" as a generic name. Many manufacturers in the southwestern Shandong area produce bedding, crafts, and clothing using Lujin fabric, and these manufacturers may legitimately use the name "Lujin" to descriptively indicate that their products use Lujin fabric.

In this case, Juancheng Lujin Company used the characters "Lujin" on the packaging boxes and packaging bags of the products involved, and although it used the generic name for goods contained in Lujin Company's trademark on its products, this was solely to indicate that its products adopted Lujin fabric and that its production technique possessed the characteristics of Lujin. It did not have subjective malice to infringe Lujin Company's exclusive right to use the registered trademark "Lujin", nor was it used as a commercial identifier. This constituted fair use and therefore should not be deemed an infringement of the exclusive right to use the registered trademark "Lujin". For the same reason, the use of the characters "Lujin" in Juancheng Lujin Company's enterprise name also constituted fair use and did not constitute unfair competition. Lizhibang Company, as a specialty store for Lujin products, equally had the right to use the characters "Lujin", and also did not constitute an infringement of the exclusive right to use the registered trademark "Lujin".

Furthermore, Lujin Company's word trademark "Lujin" and the combined trademark "Lj+LUJIN" had been approved for registration by the State Trademark Office and approved for use on goods in Class 25 and Class 24, and the exclusive right to use these registered trademarks should be protected by law. Although Juancheng Lujin Company had applied for cancellation of this trademark, before the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board under the State Trademark Office revoked it, the valid registered trademark should still be protected by law. Given that "Lujin" is a registered trademark, in order to regulate market order and protect fair competition, while Juancheng Lujin Company uses the characters "Lujin" in the future to indicate the fabric nature of its products, it should reasonably avoid Lujin Company's exclusive right to use the registered trademark, and should prominently use its own "Jingyifang" trademark on its product packaging to clearly distinguish the source of the products and facilitate consumer identification.

Guiding Case No. 47: Ferrero S.p.A. v. Montesha (Zhangjiagang) Food Co., Ltd. and Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area Zhengyuan Marketing Co., Ltd. — dispute over unfair competition

(Discussed and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on April 15, 2015)

Keywords
Civil; unfair competition; well-known goods; distinctive packaging and decoration

Ruling Gist

1. A well-known good as referred to in the Anti-Unfair Competition Law means a good that has a certain market reputation in China and is known to the relevant public. For goods that are known internationally, the protection of their distinctive names, packaging, and decoration in China must still be based on the necessity that they are known to the relevant public within China. Therefore, the determination of such a well-known good should take into account factors such as the time, region, volume, and target of sales of the good in China; the duration, extent, and geographic scope of its promotion; its protection as a well-known good; and appropriate consideration of its international reputation, for a comprehensive assessment.

2. The distinctive packaging and decoration of a well-known good protected under the Anti-Unfair Competition Law refer to the containers and other packaging used to contain or protect the good, which can distinguish the source of the good, as well as the decoration composed of text, patterns, colors, and their arrangements attached to the good or its packaging, which can distinguish the source of the good.

3. Full-scale imitation of another person's distinctive packaging and decoration of a well-known good that can distinguish the source of the good, to an extent sufficient to cause market confusion or misidentification, constitutes an act of unfair competition.

Relevant Legal Provision

Article 5, item 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the PRC

Basic Facts

Plaintiff Ferrero S.p.A. (Italy) (hereinafter referred to as Ferrero Company) alleged that the defendant Montesha (Zhangjiagang) Food Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Montesha Company) imitated the plaintiff's products, and without authorization used packaging and decoration identical or similar to the distinctive packaging and decoration of the plaintiff's well-known goods, causing confusion among consumers. The above conduct of the defendant Montesha Company and the sale of imitative products by the defendant Tianjin Economic-Technological Development Area Zhengyuan Marketing Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Zhengyuan Company) had caused significant economic losses to the plaintiff. The plaintiff requested that the court order Montesha Company not to produce or sell, and Zhengyuan Company not to sell, any chocolate products that comply with any one or any combination of the distinctive packaging and decoration of Ferrero Company's chocolate products, or any chocolate products similar to Ferrero Company's above packaging and decoration sufficient to cause consumer misidentification, and to apologize, eliminate the impact, bear litigation costs, and that Montesha Company pay 3 million yuan in damages.

Defendant Montesha Company argued that the plaintiff's products involved in the case were not known to the relevant public in the Chinese market, while the Jinsha chocolate products produced by Montesha Company enjoyed high reputation among Chinese consumers and were well-known goods. The packaging and decoration for which the plaintiff sought protection were common packaging and decoration for similar chocolate products domestically and internationally, lacking originality and specificity. The packaging and decoration used by Montesha Company for its Jinsha chocolate were developed in cooperation with professional designers and were not imitations of others' existing packaging and decoration. Ordinary consumers, upon exercising ordinary attention, would not confuse the chocolate products produced by each party. The plaintiff argued that its product packaging encompassed multiple intellectual property rights, including trademarks, designs, and copyrights, but did not specifically indicate which rights were infringed by the packaging and decoration of the allegedly infringing products. The object of the plaintiff's claim was vague. Therefore, the plaintiff's complaint lacked factual and legal basis, and the defendant requested the dismissal of the plaintiff's claims.

Facts Found by the Court: Ferrero Company was established in Italy in 1946. Its Ferrero Rocher chocolates were launched on the market in 1982 and had been advertised on television, in newspapers, and in magazines in several Asian countries and regions. In the Taiwan and Hong Kong regions of China, Ferrero Rocher chocolates were named "Jinsha" chocolates and were registered as the "Jinsha" trademark in Taiwan in June 1990 and in Hong Kong in 1993. In February 1984, Ferrero Rocher chocolates entered the domestic market through consignment sales by China National Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Import and Export Corporation, primarily sold in duty-free shops and airport stores, as permitted by the then-current policies, and continued until approximately 1993. In October 1986, Ferrero Company registered the "FERRERO ROCHER" trademark and the graphic (oval lace pattern) and their combination series of trademarks in China, and used them on chocolate products sold within China. The main features of the packaging and decoration used for Ferrero Rocher chocolates are: 1. Each spherical chocolate is wrapped in gold foil paper; 2. On the golden spherical wrapper, an oval gold-edged label printed with the "FERRERO ROCHER" trademark is affixed as decoration; 3. Each golden spherical chocolate has a brown paper base tray as decoration; 4. Several shapes of transparent plastic packaging are used to display the golden spherical inner packaging; 5. The transparent plastic packaging uses an oval gold-edged pattern as decoration, with a product image and trademark inside the oval, and a red-gold ribbon pattern extending from the trademark. Three-dimensional packaging for Ferrero Rocher chocolate products in 8-piece, 16-piece, 24-piece, and 30-piece configurations was applied for as three-dimensional trademarks at the World Intellectual Property Organization in 1984. Starting in 1993, Ferrero Company gradually increased advertising for Ferrero Rocher chocolates in domestic newspapers, periodicals, and outdoor advertisements, focusing on the Guangdong, Shanghai, and Beijing regions, and successively established counters in some large and medium-sized cities for sales, and enhanced the product's visibility by sponsoring some commercial and sports activities. In June 2000, its "FERRERO ROCHER" trademark was included in the National Key Trademark Protection List by the State Administration for Industry and Commerce. The administrative departments for industry and commerce in Guangdong, Hebei, and other places in China had repeatedly investigated and punished acts of imitating the packaging and decoration of Ferrero Rocher chocolates.

Mengtesha Company was a Sino-foreign joint venture established in December 1991 by Zhangjiagang No.1 Dairy Factory and Belgium Fetadale Co., Ltd., producing and selling various types of molded chocolates. Zhangjiagang No.1 Dairy Factory began producing Jinsha chocolates in 1990, and applied to register the "Jinsha" word mark on April 23, 1990, which was approved for registration by the Trademark Office of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce in April 1991. In 2002, Zhangjiagang No.1 Dairy Factory transferred the "Jinsha" trademark to Mengtesha Company, filing an application on November 25, 2002, and the transfer was approved by the Trademark Office of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce on April 21, 2004. From then on, Mengtesha Company began producing and selling Jinsha chocolates. When producing and selling Jinsha chocolate products, although Mengtesha Company replaced "Jinsha" with the combined trademark "Jinsha TRESOR DORE," it continued to use the packaging and decoration used by Zhangjiagang No.1 Dairy Factory for its Jinsha chocolate products. The packaging and decoration of the allegedly infringing Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolates are: each Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate is spherical and wrapped in gold foil; on top of each golden spherical wrapper, an oval gold-edged label printed with the "Jinsha TRESOR DORE" trademark is affixed; each golden spherical chocolate is accompanied by a bowl-shaped brown paper base tray with a smooth, wrinkle-free bottom and wavy pleats on the side; the outer packaging is transparent plastic paper or a plastic box; in the center of the outer packaging, an oval gold-edged pattern is used, containing a product image and the Jinsha TRESOR DORE trademark, from which a red-gold ribbon extends. The above features are similar in overall impression and main parts to the packaging and decoration for which Ferrero Company sought protection in its lawsuit. Zhengyuan Company was a distributor in Tianjin for the Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolates produced by Mengtesha Company. In January 2003, Ferrero Company, after notarization by the Tianjin Notary Public Office, purchased the allegedly infringing products from Zhengyuan Company in Hedong District, Tianjin.

Judgment

The Second Intermediate People's Court of Tianjin rendered a civil judgment on February 7, 2005 ((2003) Er Zhong Min San Chu Zi No. 63), holding: Ferrero Company's claims against Mengtesha Company and Zhengyuan Company were dismissed. Ferrero Company appealed. The Tianjin High People's Court rendered a judgment on January 9, 2006 ((2005) Jin Gao Min San Zhong Zi No. 36), holding: 1. The first-instance judgment was reversed; 2. Mengtesha Company was ordered to immediately cease using the infringing packaging and decoration for the Jinsha TRESOR DORE series of chocolates; 3. Mengtesha Company was ordered to pay Ferrero Company RMB 700,000 as compensation, to be paid within fifteen days after the judgment took effect; 4. Zhengyuan Company was ordered to immediately cease selling the Jinsha TRESOR DORE series of chocolates using the infringing packaging and decoration; 5. Ferrero Company's other claims were dismissed. Mengtesha Company, dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, filed a petition for retrial with the Supreme People's Court. The Supreme People's Court rendered a civil judgment on March 24, 2008 ((2006) Min San Ti Zi No. 3), holding: 1. Items 1 and 5 of the civil judgment of the Tianjin High People's Court ((2005) Jin Gao Min San Zhong Zi No. 36) were affirmed; 2. Item 2 of the civil judgment of the Tianjin High People's Court ((2005) Jin Gao Min San Zhong Zi No. 36) was modified as follows: Mengtesha Company was ordered to immediately cease the unfair competition act of using packaging and decoration on its Jinsha TRESOR DORE series of chocolate products that are similar to the distinctive packaging and decoration of Ferrero's series of chocolate products; 3. Item 3 of the civil judgment of the Tianjin High People's Court ((2005) Jin Gao Min San Zhong Zi No. 36) was modified as follows: Mengtesha Company was ordered to pay Ferrero Company RMB 500,000 in compensation within fifteen days after the service of this judgment; 4. Item 4 of the civil judgment of the Tianjin High People's Court ((2005) Jin Gao Min San Zhong Zi No. 36) was modified as follows: Zhengyuan Company was ordered to immediately cease selling the above Jinsha TRESOR DORE series of chocolate products.

Reasoning

The Supreme People's Court held: This case primarily involves the following disputed issues: whether Ferrero Rocher chocolates are prior well-known goods, whether the packaging and decoration used by Ferrero Rocher chocolates are distinctive packaging and decoration, and whether the use of packaging and decoration by Mengtesha Company on its Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolates constitutes unfair competition.

I. Whether Ferrero Rocher chocolates are prior well-known goods

Based on evidence such as the consignment contract and confirmation letters of consignment contracts between China National Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Import and Export Corporation and Ferrero Company, the court of second instance correctly found that Ferrero Rocher chocolates had been sold within China since 1984. Well-known goods under the Anti-Unfair Competition Law refer to goods that have a certain degree of market reputation within China and are known to the relevant public. For goods that are internationally known, the protection of their distinctive names, packaging, and decoration under Chinese law still requires that they be known to the relevant public within China. The reputation claimed for goods or services is usually generated from production, sale, or other business activities within China. To determine whether goods are well-known, factors such as the time, region, volume, and targets of sales; the duration, extent, and geographic scope of advertising; and the record of protection as well-known goods should be comprehensively considered; it is also not excluded that international renown may be appropriately taken into account. In the second-instance judgment, the statement that "the evaluation of the well-known status of goods should be comprehensively determined based on their fame in specific markets both domestically and internationally, and should not be understood as referring only to goods well-known within China" was inappropriate. However, based on the time Ferrero Rocher chocolates entered the Chinese market, their sales circumstances, and the various promotional activities conducted by Ferrero Company, the finding that they are well-known goods with a relatively high reputation in the relevant market within China was correct. Mengtesha Company's claim that Ferrero Rocher chocolates became well-known in the Chinese market later than Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolates cannot be sustained. Furthermore, Ferrero Company used its packaging and decoration for Ferrero Rocher chocolates first. Mengtesha Company's claim that the packaging and decoration it used were independently developed lacks sufficient evidentiary support. The second-instance judgment correctly found that Mengtesha Company misappropriated the distinctive packaging and decoration of Ferrero Rocher chocolates.

II. Whether the packaging and decoration used for Ferrero Rocher chocolates are distinctive

Containers such as packaging that hold or protect goods, as well as the decoration consisting of text, designs, colors, and their arrangements attached to the goods or their packaging, are protected as distinctive packaging and decoration under the Anti-Unfair Competition Law when they can distinguish the source of the goods. The packaging and decoration for which Ferrero Company sought protection, as used for Ferrero Rocher chocolates, consist of a series of elements. If the packaging and decoration were formed merely by a simple combination of wrapping spherical chocolates in tin foil, using transparent plastic outer packaging, and displaying the inner chocolate packaging, they would lack distinctiveness to distinguish the source of the goods and would not be considered distinctive; moreover, each element in such a combination is also a generic packaging and decoration element in the food packaging industry and cannot be exclusively used. However, there is a wide range of choices in the arrangement of packaging materials such as tin foil, paper trays, and plastic boxes in terms of shape and color; there is also great design freedom in the size, design, and composition of the trademark label attached to the packaging. Within the scope of free design, a unique combination of the various elements of packaging and decoration that gives them significant features to distinguish the source of the goods can constitute distinctive packaging and decoration for the goods. The packaging and decoration used for Ferrero Rocher chocolates, due to the unique arrangement of their constituent elements in terms of text, design, color, shape, and size, form a distinctive overall image, which is unrelated to the functionality of the goods. After extensive use and substantial promotion, they are sufficient to lead the relevant public to associate the overall image of the packaging and decoration with Ferrero Company's Ferrero Rocher chocolate products, thereby serving to identify the source of the goods, and thus they fall within the scope of distinctive packaging and decoration protected under item (2) of Article 5 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law. Mengtesha Company's argument that finding the packaging and decoration in question as distinctive would cause generic packaging and decoration in the chocolate industry to be exclusively used by Ferrero Company, monopolizing the domestic spherical chocolate market, cannot be sustained.

III. Whether the relevant public is likely to confuse or mistake Ferrero Rocher chocolates for Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolates

In the design of product packaging and decoration, different business operators may learn from and draw on each other's designs and engage in innovative designs to create packaging and decoration that distinguish their products. This is a necessary requirement of market operations and competition. In this case, Mengtesha Company could have fully utilized the generic elements in chocolate packaging and decoration design to freely design packaging and decoration clearly distinct from the distinctive packaging and decoration used earlier by others. However, it must not completely imitate the distinctive packaging and decoration of others that serve to identify the source of goods in a manner likely to cause market confusion or mistake; otherwise, it would constitute unfair competition. The confusion or mistake under the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of China refers to circumstances sufficient to cause the relevant public to be mistaken as to the source of the goods, including mistakenly believing that there is a licensing relationship, affiliated enterprise relationship, or other specific connection with the business operator of the well-known goods. In this case, because the overall image of the packaging and decoration used by Ferrero Rocher chocolates has distinct features for distinguishing the source of the goods, and the packaging and decoration used by Mengtesha Company on its chocolate products are visually very similar to Ferrero's distinctive packaging and decoration, even if there are differences between the two products in terms of price, quality, taste, consumer level, and differing manufacturer names and trademarks, it is still not sufficient to prevent the relevant public from easily mistaking that there is some economic connection between Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolates and Ferrero Rocher chocolates. Accordingly, the petitioner's argument that the similar packaging and decoration in this case would not cause consumer confusion or mistake cannot be sustained.

In summary, on the Jinsha TRESOR DORE chocolate products produced by Mengtesha Company, it misappropriated packaging and decoration similar to Ferrero Company's distinctive packaging and decoration for Ferrero Rocher chocolates, sufficient to cause the relevant public to confuse or mistake the source of the goods, thereby constituting unfair competition.

Guiding Case No. 48: Beijing Jingdiao Technology Co., Ltd. v. Shanghai Naikai Electronic Technology Co., Ltd. — dispute over infringement of computer software copyright

(Released by the Adjudication Committee of the Supreme People's Court on April 15, 2015)

Keywords: Civil, infringement of computer software copyright, bundling sales, technological protection measures, abuse of rights

Ruling Gist

Where a computer software copyright holder, with the aim of bundling the software with a machine, sets the output data of the software to a specific file format so as to restrict other competitors' machines from reading data stored in that specific file format, thereby extending the software's competitive advantage to the machine, this does not constitute a technological measure taken by the copyright holder to protect its software copyright as provided by the Copyright Law. The act of another party developing software that reads such a specific file format does not constitute infringement of the computer software copyright.

Relevant Legal Provisions

Item (6) of Paragraph 1 of Article 48 of the Copyright Law of the PRC
Article 2, Item (1) of Paragraph 1 of Article 3, and Item (3) of Paragraph 1 of Article 24 of the Regulations on Protection of Computer Software

Basic Facts

The plaintiff, Beijing Jingdiao Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Jingdiao Company"), alleged: The plaintiff independently developed the Jingdiao CNC engraving system, which consists of three major components: Jingdiao engraving CAD/CAM software (JDPaint software), Jingdiao CNC system, and the mechanical body. The system is operated using two computers: one is the machining programming computer, and the other is the CNC control computer. The two computers run two different programs and need to exchange data, that is, through data files. Specifically, the JDPaint software is run on the machining programming computer to generate data files in Eng format, which are then received by the control software running on the CNC control computer and converted into machining instructions. The plaintiff holds the copyright in the JDPaint software, which is not sold to the public but is only equipped for use with the CNC engraving machines independently produced by the plaintiff. In early 2006, the plaintiff discovered that the defendant, Shanghai Naikai Electronic Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Naikai Company"), was actively promoting on its website that its NC-1000 engraving and milling machine numerical control system fully supported various versions of Jingdiao Eng files. The Ncstudio software in the defendant's above-mentioned numerical control system could read the Eng format data files output by the JDPaint software, and the plaintiff had encrypted the Eng format. The defendant's act of illegally decrypting the encryption measures of the Eng format, and developing and selling a numerical control system capable of reading Eng format data files, constitutes an act of intentionally circumventing or destroying the technological measures taken by the plaintiff to protect its software copyright, and constitutes infringement of the plaintiff's software copyright. The defendant's act allowed other CNC engraving machines to illegally receive Eng files, resulting in a reduction in sales of the plaintiff's Jingdiao engraving machines and causing economic losses. Therefore, the plaintiff requested the court to order the defendant to immediately cease the development, sale, and other infringing activities of the numerical control system supporting the output of Eng format from various versions of Jingdiao JDPaint, make a public apology, and compensate for losses of RMB 485,000.

Naikai Company argued: The Ncstudio software it developed could read the Eng format data files output by the JDPaint software, but the Eng data files and the Eng format used in those files do not fall within the scope of protection of computer software copyright, so the defendant's act does not constitute infringement. It requested the court to dismiss the plaintiff's claims.

The court found after trial: Jingdiao Company respectively obtained Computer Software Copyright Registration Certificates numbered Ruan Zhu Deng Zi No. 0011393 and No. 025028 from the National Copyright Administration in 2001 and 2004, certifying it as the original owner of the Jingdiao engraving software JDPaint V4.0 and JDPaint V5.0 (collectively, "JDPaint"). Naikai Company respectively obtained Computer Software Copyright Registration Certificates numbered Ruan Zhu Deng Zi No. 023060 and No. 041930 from the National Copyright Administration in 2004 and 2005, certifying it as the original owner of the software Naikai Numerical Control System V5.0 and Weihong Numerical Control Motion Control System V3.0 (collectively, "Ncstudio").

Naikai Company announced on its company website: In December 2005, Naikai Company launched the NC-1000 engraving and milling machine control system, which fully supported various versions of Jingdiao Eng files. This function was developed in response to users' fondness for the Jingdiao JDPaint V5.19 layout software.

The Eng files output by Jingdiao Company's JDPaint software are data files using the Eng format. Naikai Company's Ncstudio software can read the Eng files output by the JDPaint software, meaning that the Ncstudio software is compatible with the Eng files output by the JDPaint software.

Judgment

The First Intermediate People's Court of Shanghai rendered a civil judgment on September 20, 2006 ((2006) Hu Yi Zhong Min Wu (Zhi) Chu Zi No. 134), holding: The plaintiff Jingdiao Company's claims were dismissed. After the judgment was announced, Jingdiao Company appealed. The Shanghai High People's Court rendered a civil judgment on December 13, 2006 ((2006) Hu Gao Min San (Zhi) Zhong Zi No. 110), holding: The appeal was dismissed and the original judgment was affirmed.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held: The disputed issues to be resolved in this case are: First, whether the Eng format data files output by the plaintiff Jingdiao Company's JDPaint software, which are encrypted, fall within the scope of protection of computer software copyright; second, whether the act of Naikai Company developing software capable of reading the Eng format files output by JDPaint software constitutes the act of "intentionally circumventing or destroying technological measures taken by the copyright holder to protect its software copyright" as provided in item (6) of Paragraph 1 of Article 48 of the Copyright Law of the PRC (hereinafter "Copyright Law") and item (3) of Paragraph 1 of Article 24 of the Regulations on Protection of Computer Software.

On the first point. Article 2 of the Regulations on the Protection of Computer Software provides: "For the purposes of these Regulations, 'computer software' (hereinafter referred to as 'software') means computer programs and their associated documentation." Article 3 provides: "For the purposes of these Regulations, the following terms shall have the following meanings: (1) 'Computer program' means a code sequence of instructions that can be executed by a computer or other device with information processing capabilities to achieve a certain result, or a symbolic sequence of instructions or a symbolic sequence of statements that can be automatically converted into a code sequence of instructions. The source program and object program of the same computer program constitute the same work. (2) 'Documentation' means written materials and diagrams used to describe the content, composition, design, functional specifications, development status, test results, and usage methods of a program, such as program design specifications, flowcharts, user manuals, etc. ..." Article 4 provides: "The software protected under these Regulations must be independently developed by the developer and must be fixed on a tangible object." According to the above provisions, the scope of protection of computer software copyright is software programs and documentation.

In this case, the Eng file is a data file generated by the operation of the JDPaint software on a processing programming computer. The output format it uses, i.e., the Eng format, is the result produced by the execution of the object program of the JDPaint computer software by the computer. This data file itself is not a code sequence of instructions, a symbolic sequence of instructions, or a symbolic sequence of statements, nor can it be run and executed by a computer. The act of cracking the Eng format file itself will not directly cause illegal copying of the JDPaint software. Furthermore, the data recorded in this file is not inherent to the JDPaint software of the plaintiff, Jingdiao Company, but is generated by the software user inputting engraving processing information. These data do not belong to Jingdiao Company, the copyright owner of the JDPaint software. Therefore, the data and file format contained in the Eng format data file are not part of the program of the JDPaint software and do not fall within the scope of protection of computer software copyright.

On the second point. According to Article 48, paragraph 1, item (6) of the Copyright Law and Article 24, paragraph 1, item (3) of the Regulations on the Protection of Computer Software, the act of intentionally evading or destroying the technical measures taken by the copyright owner to protect their software copyright constitutes an act of infringing software copyright. The above provisions reflect restrictions on malicious evasion of technical measures and are protections for computer software copyright. However, the above restrictions on "malicious evasion of technical measures" cannot be abused. The above provisions mainly target malicious technical evasion acts implemented against protected software copyright. The act of a copyright owner setting a specific file format for output data and taking encryption measures on that file format to restrict machines of other brands from reading the data saved in that file format, thereby ensuring a competitive market advantage for the machines bundled with its own computer software, does not constitute an act of taking technical measures to protect software copyright as referred to in the above provisions. The act of others developing software capable of reading the specific file format set by the copyright owner does not constitute an infringement of software copyright.

According to the facts of this case, the Eng format file output by JDPaint is a file used for data exchange between two computer programs in Jingdiao Company's "Jingdiao CNC Engraving System." In terms of design purpose, Jingdiao Company adopted the Eng format instead of a common format for data exchange, not to encrypt and protect the JDPaint software, but to ensure that only the "Jingdiao CNC Engraving System" could receive this format and that only engraving machines bundled with the "Jingdiao CNC Engraving System" could use the software. Jingdiao Company's adoption of the Eng format for JDPaint output files aimed to limit the use of the JDPaint software solely within the "Jingdiao CNC Engraving System." Its fundamental purpose and true intention were to establish and consolidate the bundle relationship between the JDPaint software and its engraving machines. This act does not constitute a technical protection measure for protecting software copyright. If the protection of software copyright were extended to products bundled with the software, it would inevitably exceed the scope of protection of computer software copyright under China's copyright law. The technical measures adopted by Jingdiao Company in this case were not taken to protect the copyright of the JDPaint software, but to obtain benefits beyond copyright interests. Therefore, the technical measures taken by Jingdiao Company do not fall within the technical measures taken by the copyright owner to protect its software copyright as stipulated in the Copyright Law and the Regulations on the Protection of Computer Software. The act of Naikai Company in developing software capable of reading the Eng format files output by JDPaint software does not constitute the act of intentionally evading or destroying technical measures taken by the copyright owner to protect software copyright.

Guiding Case No. 49: Shi Honglin v. Taizhou Huaren Electronic Information Co., Ltd. — dispute over infringement of computer software copyright

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on April 15, 2015)

Keywords: civil; infringement of computer software copyright; burden of proof; infringement comparison; defective features

Ruling Gist

Where the defendant refuses to provide the source program or object program of the allegedly infringing software, and due to technical limitations, the object program cannot be directly read from the allegedly infringing product, if the software of the plaintiff and the defendant are basically the same in terms of design defects, and the defendant has no legitimate reason to refuse to provide its software source program or object program for direct comparison, then, considering the objective difficulty of the plaintiff in providing evidence, it may be determined that the computer software of the plaintiff and the defendant are substantially identical, and the defendant shall bear liability for infringement.

Related Legal Provisions

Article 3, paragraph 1, of the Regulations on the Protection of Computer Software

Basic Facts

The plaintiff, Shi Honglin, alleged: The defendant, Taizhou Huaren Electronic Information Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Huaren Company), without permission, had for a long time extensively copied, distributed, and sold software identical to Shi Honglin's computer software "S-Type Wire-Cutting Machine Tool Single-Chip Microcomputer Controller System Software V1.0," seriously infringing upon his legitimate rights and interests. Therefore, he requested the court to order Huaren Company to cease infringement, make a public apology, and compensate him for economic losses of RMB 100,000, as well as evidence preservation notarization fees, litigation agency fees of RMB 9,200, and appraisal fees incurred to stop the infringement.

The defendant, Huaren Company, argued: The system software used in its HR-Z type wire-cutting machine tool controller was independently developed by the company and could not possibly be identical to Shi Honglin's S-type wire-cutting machine tool single-chip microcomputer controller system. Moreover, the hardware and keyboard layouts of its company's product and Shi Honglin's S-type wire-cutting machine tool single-chip microcomputer controller were completely different. Huaren Company requested the dismissal of Shi Honglin's claims.

The court found through trial: On August 1, 2000, Shi Honglin completed the development of the S-type wire-cutting machine tool single-chip microcomputer controller system software. On April 18, 2005, he obtained the computer software copyright registration certificate No. 035260 from the National Copyright Administration. The certificate indicated that the software name was S-type Wire-Cutting Machine Tool Single-Chip Microcomputer Controller System Software V1.0 (hereinafter referred to as S Series Software), the copyright owner was Shi Honglin, and the method of acquisition was original acquisition. On December 20, 2005, the Hailing District Notary Office of Taizhou City issued Notarial Certificate (2005) Tai Hai Zheng Min Nei Zi No. 1146, which recorded the purchase process of Shi Honglin purchasing one HR-Z wire-cutting machine tool numerical control controller (hereinafter referred to as HR-Z type controller) from Huaren Company for RMB 660 and obtaining a sales invoice (No. 00550751). The notary office made a preservation notarization work record, took 8 photos of the purchased controller, its instruction manual, and outer packaging, and sealed the controller.

During the first instance, the court commissioned the Jiangsu Provincial Science and Technology Consulting Center to conduct a comparative appraisal on the following matters: (1) The identity of the software source program provided by Shi Honglin in this case and the software source program registered with the National Copyright Administration; (2) The similarity or identity of the software source program code of Huaren Company's HR-Z type controller preserved by notarization and the software source program code for which Shi Honglin had obtained copyright registration. Subsequently, the Jiangsu Provincial Science and Technology Consulting Center issued an appraisal work report, stating that because the defendant's software was mainly solidified on two chips, the AT89F51 from the American company ATMEL and the P89C58 from the Dutch company Philips, and the chip codenamed "AT89F51" is a self-encrypting microcontroller, its encryption system must first be cracked to read the solidified software code. However, based on the existing technical conditions, the problem of chip decryption could not be solved, making it difficult to make an objective and scientific appraisal conclusion based on the existing appraisal materials.

During the second instance, the court, upon the application of the plaintiff Shi Honglin, organized a technical appraisal on the following issues: Whether the plaintiff's software and the allegedly infringing software had the same software defects and operating characteristics. After appraisal, the Copyright Appraisal Committee of the China Copyright Protection Center issued an appraisal report, concluding that by running the plaintiff's and defendant's software, the following identical defects were found: (1) When the continuous processing program segments of both controllers exceeded 2048, both experienced abnormal execution; (2) After processing a complete program segment and setting the automatic alarm to sound only twice or less and then pressing any key to close the alarm, during the next processing cycle, before the automatic pause before the processing return line, both controllers occasionally experienced the phenomenon of the buzzer sounding twice.

The court of second instance further found: The instruction manuals for the plaintiff's and defendant's software were basically the same. The descriptions of the controller functions and technical indicators were basically the same; the instructions for use and operation were basically the same; and the paragraph arrangements and the use of most sentences were basically the same. After repeated explanations by the court of second instance, Huaren Company consistently refused to provide the source program of the allegedly infringing software for comparison.

Judgment

The Taizhou Intermediate People's Court of Jiangsu Province rendered the civil judgment (2006) Tai Min San Chu Zi No. 2 on December 8, 2006: Dismissing the plaintiff Shi Honglin's claims. Shi Honglin appealed. The Jiangsu High People's Court rendered the civil judgment (2007) Su Min San Zhong Zi No. 0018 on December 17, 2007: 1. Reversing the civil judgment (2006) Tai Min San Chu Zi No. 2 of the Taizhou Intermediate People's Court of Jiangsu Province; 2. Ordering Huaren Company to immediately cease production and sale of products infringing upon Shi Honglin's copyright in the S-type wire-cutting machine tool single-chip microcomputer controller system software V1.0; 3. Ordering Huaren Company to compensate Shi Honglin for economic losses of RMB 79,200 within 10 days of the effective date of this judgment; 4. Dismissing Shi Honglin's other claims.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that based on the existing evidence, it should be found that Huaren Company infringed Shi Honglin's copyright in the S Series Software.
