I. The standard of proof in this case should be reasonably determined based on the objective difficulty of the parties in providing evidence.

According to legal provisions, a party has the responsibility to provide evidence to prove the facts on which its claims are based. In this case, Shi Honglin claimed that Huaren Company infringed his copyright in the S Series Software. He needed to prove that the computer software of both parties was identical or substantially identical. Generally, Shi Honglin would need to prove that the source programs or object programs of the two computer software were identical or substantially identical. However, in this case, due to objective difficulties, Shi Honglin was actually unable to provide the source program or object program of the allegedly infringing HR-Z software and thereby directly prove that their source programs or object programs were identical or substantially identical. 1. Shi Honglin could not directly obtain the source program or object program of the allegedly infringing computer software. Since the source program and object program of the allegedly infringing HR-Z software were under the actual control of Huaren Company, and Huaren Company refused to provide them, Shi Honglin was actually unable to provide the source program or object program of the HR-Z software for direct comparison. 2. Existing technical means could not obtain the source program or object program of the HR-Z software from the allegedly infringing HR-Z type controller. According to the first instance appraisal situation, the object program of the HR-Z software was loaded onto the built-in chip of the HR-Z type controller. Since this chip was an encrypted chip, the object program of the HR-Z software could not be read from the chip, and the source program could not be reverse-compiled. Therefore, relying on existing technical means, the source program or object program of the HR-Z software could not be obtained from the HR-Z type controller.

In summary, in this case, where Huaren Company refused to provide the software source program for direct comparison without legitimate reason, and Shi Honglin was indeed unable to directly prove his claims due to objective difficulties, the court should, based on the principles of fairness and good faith, reasonably grasp the standard of proof and make a comprehensive judgment on whether the existing evidence provided by Shi Honglin could form a high degree of preponderance.

II. The existing evidence provided by Shi Honglin could prove that the allegedly infringing HR-Z software was substantially identical to Shi Honglin's S Series Software, and Huaren Company should bear the obligation to provide contrary evidence.

The existing evidence in this case could prove the following facts:

1. The second instance appraisal conclusion showed that by running the HX-Z software on the HX-Z type controller and the HR-Z software on the HR-Z type controller, the aforementioned identical system software defects were found in both.

2. The second instance appraisal conclusion showed that by running the HX-Z software on the HX-Z type controller and the HR-Z software on the HR-Z type controller, the same characteristic phenomena were found during power-on operation.

3. The instruction manuals for the HX-Z and HR-Z type controllers were basically the same.

4. The overall appearance and layout of the HX-Z and HR-Z type controllers were basically the same, including generally the same overall layout of the panel and keyboard.

Accordingly, given that the HX-Z and HR-Z software shared common system software defects, according to the general principles of computer software design, the probability of different software having the same software defects is extremely low when designed independently, while if software shares common software defects, the probability that their source programs are identical is relatively high. Combined with the facts that both exhibited the same characteristic phenomena during power-on operation, the instruction manuals for the HX-Z and HR-Z type controllers were basically the same, and the overall appearance and layout of the HX-Z and HR-Z type controllers were basically the same, the court held that the existing evidence provided by Shi Honglin could form a high degree of preponderance, sufficient to convince the court that the HX-Z and HR-Z software were substantially identical. Furthermore, since the HX-Z software was a revised version of Shi Honglin's S Series Software and the HX-Z software was substantially identical to the S Series Software, the allegedly infringing HR-Z software was also substantially identical to Shi Honglin's S Series Software. That is, Huaren Company infringed Shi Honglin's copyright in the S Series Software.

III. Huaren Company failed to provide contrary evidence to prove its claims and should bear the adverse consequences of failing to meet its burden of proof.

In this case, after Shi Honglin provided the above evidence to prove his claims, Huaren Company failed to provide contrary evidence to rebut them and should bear the adverse consequences of failing to meet its burden of proof according to law. After repeated explanations by this court, Huaren Company ultimately did not provide the source program of the allegedly infringing HR-Z software for comparison. Although Huaren Company provided a computer software copyright registration certificate for the DX-Z wire-cutting controller microprocessor firmware program system V3.0, it neither proved that this software was the same as the allegedly infringing HR-Z software nor proved that the completion time of the allegedly infringing HR-Z software was earlier than Shi Honglin's S Series Software or that it was independently developed by Huaren Company. Although Huaren Company also argued that a commercial sales invoice dated May 19, 2004 provided in the second instance could prove that it had completed development of the allegedly infringing software in 2004, the court held that although this invoice indicated that the goods were an HR-Z wire-cutting controller, it could not necessarily be inferred that the software used by this controller was the allegedly infringing HR-Z software, and Huaren Company did not further provide other evidence to confirm this. Combined with a series of defects such as the fact that this invoice was not a formal value-added tax invoice and did not indicate the name of the purchaser, the court held that Huaren Company's claim that it had completed development of the allegedly infringing software in 2004 lacked factual basis and was not adopted.

In conclusion, based on the existing evidence, and given that Huaren Company was in possession of the source program of the allegedly infringing HR-Z software and refused to provide it without legitimate reason, it should be determined that the allegedly infringing HR-Z software was substantially identical to Shi Honglin's S Series Software, and Huaren Company infringed Shi Honglin's copyright in the S Series Software.

Guiding Case No. 50: Li Mou, Guo Mouyang v. Guo Mouhe, Tong Moumou — dispute over inheritance

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on April 15, 2015)

Keywords: civil; inheritance; artificial insemination; children born in wedlock

Ruling Gist

1. During the existence of a marital relationship, if both parties unanimously agree to use another person's sperm for artificial insemination resulting in the wife's pregnancy, and the husband later retracts his consent, but the wife insists on giving birth to the child, regardless of whether the child is born during the existence of the marital relationship, the child shall be deemed a child born in wedlock of both spouses.

2. If a will made by one spouse does not reserve a share of the estate for a fetus, the part of the will concerning the failure to reserve such share is invalid for violating the provisions of Article 19 of the Inheritance Law of the People's Republic of China. When dividing the estate, a share of the inheritance shall be reserved for the fetus in accordance with Article 28 of the Inheritance Law of the People's Republic of China.

Related Legal Provisions

1. Article 57 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China

2. Articles 19 and 28 of the Inheritance Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

The plaintiff, Li Mou, alleged: House 306 in a residential complex in Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, was the jointly owned property of herself and the decedent, Guo Shoushun. After Guo Shoushun died of illness, her son Guo Mouyang was born. The estate of Guo Shoushun should be jointly inherited by the legal heirs, including his wife Li Mou, his son Guo Mouyang, and Guo Shoushun's parents, the defendants Guo Mouhe and Tong Moumou. She requested the court, when dividing the property and handling the inheritance, to consider that Guo Mouhe and Tong Moumou have their own real estate and retirement pensions, while Li Mou has no fixed income and must raise a young child, and to give favorable treatment to Li Mou and Guo Mouyang.

The defendants, Guo Mouhe and Tong Moumou, argued: Their son Guo Shoushun left a will before his death, clearly bequeathing House 306 to the two defendants, so statutory inheritance should not apply to this real estate. The child born to Li Mou has no blood relationship with Guo Shoushun. Guo Shoushun stated in his will that he did not want this child born through artificial insemination. After learning that he had cancer, he had already told Li Mou that he did not want this child, but Li Mou insisted on giving birth to the child. Therefore, Li Mou should be responsible for the child, and the child cannot be listed as an heir of Guo Shoushun.

法院经审理查明：1998年3月3日，原告李某与郭某顺登记结婚。2002年，郭某顺以自己的名义购买了涉案建筑面积为45.08平方米的306室房屋，并办理了房屋产权登记。2004年1月30日，李某和郭某顺共同与南京军区南京总医院生殖遗传中心签订了人工授精协议书，对李某实施了人工授精，后李某怀孕。2004年4月，郭某顺因病住院，其在得知自己患了癌症后，向李某表示不要这个孩子，但李某不同意人工流产，坚持要生下孩子。5月20日，郭某顺在医院立下自书遗嘱，在遗嘱中声明他不要这个人工授精生下的孩子，并将306室房屋赠与其父母郭某和、童某某。郭某顺于5月23日病故。李某于当年10月22日产下一子，取名郭某阳。原告李某无业，每月领取最低生活保障金，另有不固定的打工收入，并持有夫妻关系存续期间的共同存款18 705.4元。被告郭某和、童某某系郭某顺的父母，居住在同一个住宅小区的305室，均有退休工资。2001年3月，郭某顺为开店，曾向童某某借款8500元。

南京大陆房地产估价师事务所有限责任公司受法院委托，于2006年3月对涉案306室房屋进行了评估，经评估房产价值为19.3万元。

裁判结果

江苏省南京市秦淮区人民法院于2006年4月20日作出一审判决：涉案的306室房屋归原告李某所有；李某于本判决生效之日起30日内，给付原告郭某阳33 442.4元，该款由郭某阳的法定代理人李某保管；李某于本判决生效之日起30日内，给付被告郭某和33 442．4元、给付被告童某某41 942．4元。一审宣判后，双方当事人均未提出上诉，判决已发生法律效力。

裁判理由

法院生效裁判认为：本案争议焦点主要有两方面：一是郭某阳是否为郭某顺和李某的婚生子女？二是在郭某顺留有遗嘱的情况下，对306室房屋应如何析产继承？

关于争议焦点一。《最高人民法院关于夫妻离婚后人工授精所生子女的法律地位如何确定的复函》中指出：“在夫妻关系存续期间，双方一致同意进行人工授精，所生子女应视为夫妻双方的婚生子女，父母子女之间权利义务关系适用《中华人民共和国婚姻法》的有关规定。”郭某顺因无生育能力，签字同意医院为其妻子即原告李某施行人工授精手术，该行为表明郭某顺具有通过人工授精方法获得其与李某共同子女的意思表示。只要在夫妻关系存续期间，夫妻双方同意通过人工授精生育子女，所生子女均应视为夫妻双方的婚生子女。《中华人民共和国民法通则》第五十七条规定：“民事法律行为从成立时起具有法律约束力。行为人非依法律规定或者取得对方同意，不得擅自变更或者解除。”因此,郭某顺在遗嘱中否认其与李某所怀胎儿的亲子关系，是无效民事行为，应当认定郭某阳是郭某顺和李某的婚生子女。

关于争议焦点二。《中华人民共和国继承法》（以下简称《继承法》）第五条规定：“继承开始后，按照法定继承办理；有遗嘱的,按照遗嘱继承或者遗赠办理；有遗赠扶养协议的，按照协议办理。”被继承人郭某顺死亡后，继承开始。鉴于郭某顺留有遗嘱，本案应当按照遗嘱继承办理。《继承法》第二十六条规定：“夫妻在婚姻关系存续期间所得的共同所有的财产，除有约定的以外，如果分割遗产，应当先将共同所有的财产的一半分出为配偶所有，其余的为被继承人的遗产。”最高人民法院《关于贯彻执行〈中华人民共和国继承法〉若干问题的意见》第38条规定：“遗嘱人以遗嘱处分了属于国家、集体或他人所有的财产，遗嘱的这部分，应认定无效。”登记在被继承人郭某顺名下的306室房屋，已查明是郭某顺与原告李某夫妻关系存续期间取得的夫妻共同财产。郭某顺死亡后，该房屋的一半应归李某所有，另一半才能作为郭某顺的遗产。郭某顺在遗嘱中，将306室全部房产处分归其父母，侵害了李某的房产权，遗嘱的这部分应属无效。此外，《继承法》第十九条规定：“遗嘱应当对缺乏劳动能力又没有生活来源的继承人保留必要的遗产份额。”郭某顺在立遗嘱时，明知其妻子腹中的胎儿而没有在遗嘱中为胎儿保留必要的遗产份额，该部分遗嘱内容无效。《继承法》第二十八条规定：“遗产分割时，应当保留胎儿的继承份额。”因此，在分割遗产时，应当为该胎儿保留继承份额。综上，在扣除应当归李某所有的财产和应当为胎儿保留的继承份额之后，郭某顺遗产的剩余部分才可以按遗嘱确定的分配原则处理。

指导案例51号阿卜杜勒·瓦希德诉中国东方航空股份有限公司航空旅客运输合同纠纷案

（最高人民法院审判委员会讨论通过2015年4月15日发布）

关键词民事   航空旅客运输合同  航班延误   告知义务   赔偿责任

裁判要点

1. 对航空旅客运输实际承运人提起的诉讼，可以选择对实际承运人或缔约承运人提起诉讼，也可以同时对实际承运人和缔约承运人提起诉讼。被诉承运人申请追加另一方承运人参加诉讼的，法院可以根据案件的实际情况决定是否准许。

2. 当不可抗力造成航班延误，致使航空公司不能将换乘其他航班的旅客按时运抵目的地时，航空公司有义务及时向换乘的旅客明确告知到达目的地后是否提供转签服务，以及在不能提供转签服务时旅客如何办理旅行手续。航空公司未履行该项义务，给换乘旅客造成损失的，应当承担赔偿责任。

3. 航空公司在打折机票上注明“不得退票，不得转签”，只是限制购买打折机票的旅客由于自身原因而不得退票和转签，不能据此剥夺旅客在支付票款后享有的乘坐航班按时抵达目的地的权利。

相关法条

《中华人民共和国民法通则》第一百四十二条

《经1955年海牙议定书修订的1929年华沙统一国际航空运输一些规则的公约》第十九条、第二十条、第二十四条第一款

《统一非立约承运人所作国际航空运输的某些规则以补充华沙公约的公约》第七条

基本案情

2004年12月29日，ABDUL WAHEED（阿卜杜勒·瓦希德,以下简称阿卜杜勒）购买了一张由香港国泰航空公司（以下简称国泰航空公司）作为出票人的机票。机票列明的航程安排为：2004年12月31日上午11点，上海起飞至香港，同日16点香港起飞至卡拉奇；2005年1月31日卡拉奇起飞至香港，同年2月1日香港起飞至上海。其中，上海与香港间的航程由中国东方航空股份有限公司（以下简称东方航空公司）实际承运，香港与卡拉奇间的航程由国泰航空公司实际承运。机票背面条款注明，该合同应遵守华沙公约所指定的有关责任的规则和限制。该机票为打折票，机票上注明“不得退票、不得转签”。

2004年12月30日下午15时起上海浦东机场下中雪，导致机场于该日22点至23点被迫关闭1小时，该日104个航班延误。31日，因飞机除冰、补班调配等原因，导致该日航班取消43架次、延误142架次，飞机出港正常率只有24.1%。东方航空公司的MU703航班也因为天气原因延误了3小时22分钟，导致阿卜杜勒及其家属到达香港机场后未能赶上国泰航空公司飞卡拉奇的衔接航班。东方航空公司工作人员告知阿卜杜勒只有两种处理方案：其一是阿卜杜勒等人在机场里等候3天，然后搭乘国泰航空公司的下一航班，3天费用自理；其二是阿卜杜勒等人出资，另行购买其他航空公司的机票至卡拉奇，费用为

25 000港元。阿卜杜勒当即表示无法接受该两种方案，其妻子杜琳打电话给东方航空公司，但该公司称有关工作人员已下班。杜琳对东方航空公司的处理无法接受，且因携带婴儿而焦虑、激动。最终由香港机场工作人员交涉，阿卜杜勒及家属共支付17 000港元，购买了阿联酋航空公司的机票及行李票，搭乘该公司航班绕道迪拜，到达卡拉奇。为此，阿卜杜勒支出机票款4721港元、行李票款759港元，共计5480港元。

阿卜杜勒认为，东方航空公司的航班延误，又拒绝重新安排航程，给自己造成了经济损失，遂提出诉讼，要求判令东方航空公司赔偿机票款和行李票款，并定期对外公布航班的正常率、旅客投诉率。

东方航空公司辩称，航班延误的原因系天气条件恶劣，属不可抗力；其已将此事通知了阿卜杜勒，阿卜杜勒亦明知将错过香港的衔接航班，其无权要求东方航空公司改变航程。阿卜杜勒称，其明知会错过衔接航班仍选择登上飞往香港的航班，系因为东方航空公司对其承诺会予以妥善解决。

裁判结果

上海市浦东新区人民法院于2005年12月21日作出（2005）浦民一（民）初字第12164号民事判决：一、中国东方航空股份有限公司应在判决生效之日起十日内赔偿阿卜杜勒损失共计人民币5863.60元；二、驳回阿卜杜勒的其他诉讼请求。宣判后，中国东方航空股份有限公司提出上诉。上海市第一中级人民法院于2006年2月24日作出（2006）沪一中民一（民）终字第609号民事判决：驳回上诉，维持原判。

裁判理由

法院生效裁判认为：原告阿卜杜勒是巴基斯坦国公民，其购买的机票，出发地为我国上海，目的地为巴基斯坦卡拉奇。《中华人民共和国民法通则》第一百四十二条第一款规定：“涉外民事关系的法律适用，依照本章的规定确定。”第二款规定：“中华人民共和国缔结或者参加的国际条约同中华人民共和国的民事法律有不同规定的，适用国际条约的规定，但中华人民共和国声明保留的条款除外。”我国和巴基斯坦都是《经1955年海牙议定书修订的1929年华沙统一国际航空运输一些规则的公约》（以下简称《1955年在海牙修改的华沙公约》）和1961年《统一非立约承运人所办国际航空运输的某些规则以补充华沙公约的公约》（以下简称《瓜达拉哈拉公约》）的缔约国，故这两个国际公约对本案适用。《1955年在海牙修改的华沙公约》第二十八条（1）款规定：“有关赔偿的诉讼，应该按原告的意愿，在一个缔约国的领土内，向承运人住所地或其总管理处所在地或签订契约的机构所在地法院提出，或向目的地法院提出。”第三十二条规定：“运输合同的任何条款和在损失发生以前的任何特别协议，如果运输合同各方借以违背本公约的规则，无论是选择所适用的法律或变更管辖权的规定，都不生效力。”据此，在阿卜杜勒持机票起诉的情形下，中华人民共和国上海市浦东新区人民法院有权对这起国际航空旅客运输合同纠纷进行管辖。

《瓜达拉哈拉公约》第一条第二款规定：“‘缔约承运人’指与旅客或托运人，或与旅客或托运人的代理人订立一项适用华沙公约的运输合同的当事人。”第三款规定：“‘实际承运人’指缔约承运人以外，根据缔约承运人的授权办理第二款所指的全部或部分运输的人，但对该部分运输此人并非华沙公约所指的连续承运人。在没有相反的证据时，上述授权被推定成立。”第七条规定：“对实际承运人所办运输的责任诉讼，可以由原告选择，对实际承运人或缔约承运人提起，或者同时或分别向他们提起。如果只对其中的一个承运人提起诉讼，则该承运人应有权要求另一承运人参加诉讼。这种参加诉讼的效力以及所适用的程序，根据受理案件的法院的法律决定。”阿卜杜勒所持机票，是由国泰航空公司出票，故国际航空旅客运输合同关系是在阿卜杜勒与国泰航空公司之间设立，国泰航空公司是缔约承运人。东方航空公司与阿卜杜勒之间不存在直接的国际航空旅客运输合同关系，也不是连续承运人，只是推定其根据国泰航空公司的授权，完成该机票确定的上海至香港间运输任务的实际承运人。阿卜杜勒有权选择国泰航空公司或东方航空公司或两者同时为被告提起诉讼；在阿卜杜勒只选择东方航空公司为被告提起的诉讼中，东方航空公司虽然有权要求国泰航空公司参加诉讼，但由于阿卜杜勒追究的航班延误责任发生在东方航空公司承运的上海至香港段航程中，与国泰航空公司无关，根据本案案情，衡量诉讼成本，无需追加国泰航空公司为本案的当事人共同参加诉讼。故东方航空公司虽然有权申请国泰航空公司参加诉讼，但这种申请能否被允许，应由受理案件的法院决定。一审法院认为国泰航空公司与阿卜杜勒要追究的航班延误责任无关，根据本案旅客维权的便捷性、担责可能性、诉讼的成本等情况，决定不追加香港国泰航空公司为本案的当事人，并无不当。

《1955年在海牙修改的华沙公约》第十九条规定：“承运人对旅客、行李或货物在航空运输过程中因延误而造成的损失应负责任。”第二十条（1）款规定：“承运人如果证明自己和他的代理人为了避免损失的发生，已经采取一切必要的措施，或不可能采取这种措施时，就不负责任。”2004年12月31日的MU703航班由于天气原因发生延误，对这种不可抗力造成的延误，东方航空公司不可能采取措施来避免发生，故其对延误本身无需承担责任。但还需证明其已经采取了一切必要的措施来避免延误给旅客造成的损失发生，否则即应对旅客因延误而遭受的损失承担责任。阿卜杜勒在浦东机场时由于预见到MU703航班的延误会使其错过国泰航空公司的衔接航班，曾多次向东方航空公司工作人员询问怎么办。东方航空公司应当知道国泰航空公司从香港飞往卡拉奇的衔接航班三天才有一次，更明知阿卜杜勒一行携带着婴儿，不便在中转机场长时间等候，有义务向阿卜杜勒一行提醒中转时可能发生的不利情形，劝告阿卜杜勒一行改日乘机。但东方航空公司没有这样做，却让阿卜杜勒填写《续航情况登记表》，并告知会帮助解决，使阿卜杜勒对该公司产生合理信赖，从而放心登机飞赴香港。鉴于阿卜杜勒一行是得到东方航空公司的帮助承诺后来到香港，但是东方航空公司不考虑阿卜杜勒一行携带婴儿要尽快飞往卡拉奇的合理需要，向阿卜杜勒告知了要么等待三天乘坐下一航班且三天中相关费用自理，要么自费购买其他航空公司机票的“帮助解决”方案。根据查明的事实，东方航空公司始终未能提供阿卜杜勒的妻子杜琳在登机前填写的《续航情况登记表》，无法证明阿卜杜勒系在明知飞往香港后会发生对己不利的情况仍选择登机，故法院认定“东方航空公司没有为避免损失采取了必要的措施”是正确的。东方航空公司没有采取一切必要的措施来避免因航班延误给旅客造成的损失发生，不应免责。阿卜杜勒迫于无奈自费购买其他航空公司的机票，对阿卜杜勒购票支出的5480港元损失，东方航空公司应承担赔偿责任。

After the delayed flight arrived at Hong Kong Airport, China Eastern Airlines refused to endorse Abdul's ticket, claiming that Abdul's ticket was a discounted ticket marked "non-refundable, non-endorsable" and that it did not need to separately remind or inform him. The court held that even if an airline states "non-refundable, non-endorsable" on a discounted ticket, this only restricts passengers who purchase discounted tickets from refunding or endorsing the ticket due to their own reasons; a passenger who purchases a discounted ticket pays the full fare, and the airline must provide complete transportation services, and cannot deprive the passenger of the right to take the flight and arrive at the destination on time after paying the fare. The flight delay in this case was not caused by Abdul's own reasons. After Abdul arrived at Hong Kong Airport on the delayed flight, he certainly needed to have his ticket re-endorsed; China Eastern Airlines neither informed Abdul at the departure airport that the ticket could not be endorsed due to the flight delay, nor did it handle the endorsement procedures for him at the transit airport. Therefore, China Eastern Airlines failed to provide evidence that the loss was caused by Abdul's own reasons, and also failed to prove that it took necessary measures and proper remedial actions to avoid the expansion of the loss. Accordingly, the court ordered China Eastern Airlines to bear liability for compensation.

Guiding Case No. 52: Hainan Fenghai Grain & Oil Industrial Co., Ltd. v. People's Insurance Company of China, Hainan Province Branch — dispute over marine cargo transportation insurance contract

(Discussed and adopted by the Adjudication Committee of the Supreme People's Court, promulgated on April 15, 2015)

Keywords: civil, maritime, marine cargo transportation, insurance contract, all risks, external cause

Ruling Gist

"All risks" in a marine cargo transportation insurance contract, in addition to covering the liabilities of free of particular average (FPA) and with average (WA), also covers all or partial loss of the insured cargo caused by external causes during transit. Where the insured is not intentionally or negligently at fault, if the loss of the insured cargo is caused by other causes not listed in the exclusion clauses of the relevant insurance contract, such causes may be determined as "external causes" resulting in the loss of the insured cargo, and the insurer shall be liable for all losses caused by such external causes during transit.

Relevant Law

Insurance Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 30

Basic Facts

On November 28, 1995, Hainan Fenghai Grain & Oil Industrial Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Fenghai Company") insured with People's Insurance Company of China, Hainan Province Branch (hereinafter "PICC Hainan") 4,999.85 tons of palm oil in drums, carried by the Indonesian-flag vessel "HAGAAG" from Dumai Port, Indonesia to Yangpu Port, China. The insurance cover was all risks, the cargo value was USD 3,574,892.75, the sum insured was USD 3,951,258, and the premium was USD 18,966. After taking out the insurance, Fenghai Company paid the premium to PICC Hainan as agreed. PICC Hainan issued a notice of shipment, issued a marine cargo insurance policy, and attached the marine cargo insurance clauses to the policy. According to the insurance clauses, the scope of cover for all risks included not only the liabilities of FPA and WA, but also PICC Hainan's responsibility for "all or partial loss of the insured cargo caused by external causes during transit." The clauses also listed five exclusion clauses. The above insured cargo was purchased by Fenghai Company from Singapore Fengyi Private Limited (hereinafter "Fengyi Company") on a CNF basis. Pursuant to the sales contract, the shipper Fengyi Company entered into a charter party with the vessel's agent, Liang International Agency Limited (hereinafter "Liang International"). The charter party stipulated that the "HAGAAG" would carry 5,000 tons of palm oil insured by Fenghai Company to Yangpu Port, China, and another 1,000 tons of palm oil to Hong Kong.

On November 29, 1995, the time charterer of the "HAGAAG" and the actual carrier of the cargo, PT. SAMUDERA INDRA of Indonesia (hereinafter "PSI Company"), issued a shipped bill of lading numbered DM/YPU/1490/95. The bill of lading stated the vessel as "HAGAAG", port of loading as Dumai Port, Indonesia, port of discharge as Yangpu Port, China, cargo marks as BATCH NO.80211/95, shipped quantity as 4,999.85 tons, clean, freight prepaid. According to investigation, the shipper Fengyi Company paid the freight to Liang International, which paid the freight to PSI Company. On December 14, 1995, Fenghai Company paid its issuing bank and took delivery of the documents, obtaining the full set (three originals) of the above insured cargo's bills of lading. From November 23 to 29, 1995, after the "HAGAAG" loaded 31,623 drums, net weight 5,999.82 tons, of Sihai brand palm oil at Dumai Port and set sail, due to a dispute over charter hire between the shipowner of the "HAGAAG", PT. PERUSAHAAN PELAYARAN BAHTERA BINTANG SELATAN of Indonesia (hereinafter "BBS Company"), and the time charterer, PSI Company, the "HAGAAG" suspended the voyage agreed in the bill of lading and blocked information on the vessel's movements.

To avoid loss of the insured cargo, Fengyi Company, Fenghai Company, and PICC Hainan repeatedly sent representatives to participate in negotiations between the shipowner and the time charterer, but as the shipowner refused to disclose the whereabouts of the "HAGAAG" on the grounds of non-receipt of hire, the multi-party talks yielded no results. Thereafter, Fengyi Company and Fenghai Company communicated through multiple channels and searched extensively for the "HAGAAG", and PICC Hainan also assisted in the search through its overseas offices. It was not until April 1996 that the "HAGAAG" was smuggled to Shanwei, China, and was seized by the Chinese maritime police. According to the Determination on Exemption from Prosecution (No. 64 (1996) of the Guangzhou People's Procuratorate, Criminal Exemption), from January to March 1996, the captain of the "HAGAAG", Ellis Lumbak, acting on instructions from BBS Company, directed the crew to transship 11,325 drums, over 2,100 tons, of palm oil onto the "IVANA" and "SALAH" cargo vessels belonging to the same shipowning company, which were then carried away and sold, and also had the crew change the vessel's name from "HAGAAG" to "ELIZA II". In April 1996, the cargo vessel renamed "ELIZA II", carrying the remaining 20,298 drums of palm oil, was smuggled into Shanwei, China, and was seized by the Chinese maritime police on April 16. The above 20,298 drums of palm oil were confiscated by the Guangdong Provincial Procuratorial Authority as smuggled goods and turned over to the state treasury. On June 6, 1996, Fenghai Company submitted a claim report to PICC Hainan. On August 20, 1996, Fenghai Company again submitted a written claim to PICC Hainan, and PICC Hainan explicitly refused to pay the claim. Fenghai Company then filed a lawsuit with the Haikou Maritime Court.

Fenghai Company was a Sino-foreign equity joint venture established on August 14, 1995, by Hainan Fengyuan Trade Development Co., Ltd. and Singapore Haiyuan International Co., Ltd. After its establishment, it established a business relationship with PICC Hainan. From October 1, 1995 to November 28, 1995 (before the issuance of the insurance policy in this case), four import palm oil insurance transactions had occurred, three of which covered all risks and one covered "all risks plus war risks." Claims were made on all four insurance transactions, including payments for cargo shortages and leakage within the scope of all risks.

Judgment

The Haikou Maritime Court rendered a civil judgment (No. 096 [1996], Hai Shang Chu Zi) on December 25, 1996: 1. PICC Hainan shall compensate Fenghai Company for the loss of insured value in the amount of USD 3,593,858.75; 2. Fenghai Company's other claims were dismissed. After the judgment was announced, PICC Hainan appealed. The Hainan High People's Court rendered a civil judgment (No. 44 [1997], Qiong Jing Zhong Zi) on October 27, 1997: the first instance judgment was reversed, and Fenghai Company's claims were dismissed. Fenghai Company applied to the Supreme People's Court for retrial. The Supreme People's Court rendered a civil ruling (No. 35 [2003], Min Si Jian Zi) on August 11, 2003, deciding to bring the case to trial, and rendered a civil judgment (No. 5 [2003], Min Si Ti Zi) on July 13, 2004: 1. The civil judgment (No. 44 [1997], Qiong Jing Zhong Zi) of the Hainan High People's Court was set aside; 2. The civil judgment (No. 096 [1996], Hai Shang Chu Zi) of the Haikou Maritime Court was affirmed.

Reasoning

The Supreme People's Court held that this case is a dispute over an international marine cargo transportation insurance contract. The insured and the destination port of the insured cargo are both within the territory of the People's Republic of China. The original trial's application of PRC law as the governing law for resolving this dispute was correct, and both parties had no objection to this.

The insurance contract concluded between Fenghai Company and PICC Hainan was legal and valid, and the rights and obligations of the parties shall be bound by the insurance policy and the attached insurance clauses. The subject matter of the insurance in this case had suffered an actual total loss. The shipper Fengyi Company was not at fault for this, nor was there evidence that the insured Fenghai Company acted intentionally or negligently. The loss of the subject matter of the insurance was caused by the rent dispute between the BBS Company, the shipowner of the "HAGAAG", and the time charterer, resulting in the shipowner taking away and selling the cargo on board and smuggling it. The focus of the dispute in this case is how to understand the scope of liability for all risks under the insurance clauses in question.

During the second instance trial, the Hainan High People's Court held that, according to the insurance clauses attached to the policy and industry practice, the scope of liability for all risks includes FPA, WA, and ordinary additional risks (i.e., theft, pilferage and non-delivery; fresh water rain damage; shortage; contamination; leakage; clashing and breakage; taint of odor; sweating and heating; hook damage; breakage of packing; rust damage). The reply of the People's Bank of China, "Reply on the Request for Interpretation of Clauses of Marine Cargo Insurance 'All Risks'", also made the same clear stipulation. It can be seen that the loss of the cargo insured by Fenghai Company does not fall within the scope of liability for all risks. In addition, given the long-term insurance business relationship between PICC Hainan and Fenghai Company, and that prior to the occurrence of this dispute, the parties had entered into multiple insurance contracts, and PICC Hainan had made payments within the scope of all risks, Fenghai Company should have been clear about the main content of the insurance contract in this case, the exclusion clauses, and the scope of liability for all risks. Therefore, the first instance judgment was found to have incorrectly applied the law.

According to the provisions of the "Marine Cargo Insurance Clauses" involved, all risks, in addition to covering the liabilities of FPA and WA, also covers losses caused by various external causes during transit. At the same time, the insurance clauses explicitly list five categories of exclusions: (1) losses caused by the intentional act or fault of the insured; (2) losses arising from the shipper's liability; (3) losses caused by existing poor quality or shortage in quantity of the insured cargo before the insurance coverage attaches; (4) losses caused by natural wear and tear, inherent defect, characteristics of the insured cargo, market price decline, or delay in transit; (5) the scope of liability and exclusions stipulated in the Company's Marine Cargo War Risks Clauses and Cargo Strike Clauses. From the above insurance clauses, the all risks clause in the marine cargo insurance clauses has the following characteristics:

1. All risks is not a list of enumerated risks, but a non-enumerated risk. In the marine cargo insurance clauses, FPA and WA are enumerated risks, while all risks is FPA plus WA plus unlisted losses of the subject matter caused by external causes during transit.

2. The loss of the subject matter must be caused by external causes. When claiming insurance compensation from the insurer, the insured must prove that the loss of the subject matter was caused by external causes during transit. External causes may be natural causes or accidental man-made incidents. However, the risks covered by all risks are uncertain, requiring coverage of risks that are uncertain, accidental, and unable to be enumerated. For those anticipated, certain, and normal perils, they do not fall within the scope of liability for external causes.

3. External causes should be limited to those occurring during transit, excluding accidents occurring before transit begins or after transit ends. As long as the insured proves that the loss was not due to its own reasons but was caused by an accident during transit, the insurer shall bear the insurance compensation liability.

According to the provisions of the Insurance Law, if an insurance contract contains clauses excluding the insurer's liability, the insurer shall clearly explain such clauses to the applicant when concluding the contract; if not clearly explained, such clauses shall not be effective. Accordingly, although the exclusions listed in the insurance clauses are not within the scope of the insurer's compensation, this is premised on the insurer having explicitly informed the insured of the exclusion clauses at the time of concluding the insurance contract. Otherwise, such exclusion clauses cannot be binding on the insured.

Regarding the reply opinion of the People's Bank of China. Before the establishment of the China Insurance Regulatory Commission, the People's Bank of China was the administrative authority for the insurance industry. On May 1, 1997, the People's Bank of China issued a "Reply on the Request for Interpretation of Clauses of Marine Cargo Insurance 'All Risks'" to the People's Insurance Company of China, stating that the scope of cover for all risks is FPA, WA, and all or partial loss of the insured cargo caused by external causes during transit. It further stated that external causes only refer to theft, pilferage and non-delivery, fresh water rain damage, etc. On November 27, 1998, the People's Bank of China, in a reply to "China Property Insurance Co., Ltd.'s Request for Interpretation of Marine Cargo Insurance Clauses", again clarified that the scope of liability for all risks includes FPA, WA, and all or partial loss of the insured cargo caused by external causes during transit. Among them, all or partial loss caused by external causes refers to 11 types of general additional risks. Since the above replies of the People's Bank of China are not laws or regulations, nor do they fall under administrative rules. According to the provisions of the Legislation Law of the People's Republic of China, the ministries and commissions under the State Council, the People's Bank of China, the National Audit Office, and directly subordinate institutions with administrative functions may, in accordance with laws and the State Council's administrative regulations, decisions, and orders, formulate rules within their respective departmental authority; matters stipulated in departmental rules shall be matters implementing laws or the State Council's administrative regulations, decisions, and orders. Therefore, insurance clauses are also not within the scope of rules that functional departments have the authority to formulate. Consequently, the explanations of the People's Bank of China regarding insurance clauses cannot be used as a basis to bind the insured. In addition, the replies of the People's Bank of China regarding all risks constitute interpretations of insurance contract clauses. For insurance contracts concluded between equal parties, only the people's court and arbitration institutions have the authority to make interpretations binding on the parties according to law. Therefore, the above replies cannot bind the insured. To make the interpretation in such replies binding on the insured as contract clauses, it could only be done by attaching them as part of the insurance contract in the policy. The very reason why the People's Insurance Company of China sought clarification from the competent authority on the scope of liability for all risks, and the authority made a reply, precisely demonstrates that there is controversy over the understanding of all risks. Pursuant to Article 31 of the Insurance Law, when there is a dispute between the insurer and the applicant, insured, or beneficiary over the terms of an insurance contract, the people's court or arbitration institution shall interpret the terms in favor of the insured or beneficiary. An interpretation favorable to its own industry made by an industry competent authority cannot be applied to a contracting party outside that industry.

In summary, it should be determined that the insurance accident in this case falls within the scope of liability for all risks. The second instance court erred in finding that the loss of the cargo insured by Fenghai Company did not fall within the scope of liability for all risks, and this should be corrected. Fenghai Company's reasons for retrial are well-founded and should be supported.
